claim: In early C. elegans embryos deficient in centralspindlin, furrows form due to an inhibitory activity that depends on aster positioning relative to the polar cortices.
source: Early C. elegans embryos deficient in the cytokinetic regulator centralspindlin form furrows, due to an inhibitory activity that depends on aster positioning relative to the polar cortices.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding of the study.

claim: Polar relaxation is associated with depletion of cortical ECT-2 specifically at the posterior cortex.
source: Here, we show polar relaxation is associated with depletion of cortical ECT-2, a RhoGEF, specifically at the posterior cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation requires intact centrosomes.
source: Asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation requires intact centrosomes, Aurora A (AIR-1), and myosin-dependent cortical flows.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation requires Aurora A (AIR-1).
source: Asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation requires intact centrosomes, Aurora A (AIR-1), and myosin-dependent cortical flows.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation requires myosin-dependent cortical flows.
source: Asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation requires intact centrosomes, Aurora A (AIR-1), and myosin-dependent cortical flows.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Three putative phospho-acceptor sites in the PH domain of ECT-2 render ECT-2 responsive to inhibition by AIR-1.
source: Within a localization competent ECT-2 fragment, we identified three putative phospho-acceptor sites in the PH domain of ECT-2 that render ECT-2 responsive to inhibition by AIR-1.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: During both polarization and cytokinesis, centrosomal AIR-1 breaks symmetry via ECT-2 phosphorylation.
source: During both polarization and cytokinesis, our results suggest that centrosomal AIR-1 breaks symmetry via ECT-2 phosphorylation; this local inhibition of ECT-2 is amplified by myosin-driven flows that generate regional ECT-2 asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of results in the abstract.

claim: Local inhibition of ECT-2 by AIR-1 is amplified by myosin-driven flows that generate regional ECT-2 asymmetry.
source: During both polarization and cytokinesis, our results suggest that centrosomal AIR-1 breaks symmetry via ECT-2 phosphorylation; this local inhibition of ECT-2 is amplified by myosin-driven flows that generate regional ECT-2 asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of results in the abstract.

claim: The active form of RhoA (C.e. RHO-1) is necessary for cleavage furrow induction.
source: The active form of the small GTPase RhoA (C.e. RHO-1) is necessary for cleavage furrow induction in these and other contexts (Kishi et al., 1993; Jantsch-Plunger et al., 2000; Zhou and Zheng, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An experimentally induced equatorial zone of active RhoA suffices to induce a furrow in cultured human cells.
source: An experimentally induced equatorial zone of active RhoA suffices to induce a furrow in cultured human cells (Wagner and Glotzer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ect2 (C.e. ECT-2) is the primary activator of RhoA during cytokinesis.
source: The guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Ect2 (C.e. ECT-2) is the primary activator of RhoA during cytokinesis (Tatsumoto et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Centralspindlin both induces relief of ECT-2 auto-inhibition and promotes Ect2 recruitment to the cortex.
source: Centralspindlin both induces relief of ECT-2 auto-inhibition and promotes Ect2 recruitment to the cortex (Yüce et al., 2005; Zhang and Glotzer, 2015; Niiya et al., 2005; Zhao and Fang, 2005; Chen et al., 2019; Su et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In early C. elegans embryos, centralspindlin functions in parallel with NOP-1 to promote ECT-2-dependent RHO-1 activation.
source: In early C. elegans embryos, centralspindlin functions in parallel with NOP-1 to promote ECT-2-dependent RHO-1 activation (Morton et al., 2012; Tse et al., 2012; Fievet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The position of the centralspindlin-dependent furrow correlates with the spindle midzone.
source: Whereas the position of the centralspindlin-dependent furrow correlates with the spindle midzone (Werner et al., 2007), the position of the NOP-1 dependent furrow anti-correlates with the position of the spindle asters (Hird and White, 1993; Dechant and Glotzer, 2003; Werner et al., 2007; Tse et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The position of the NOP-1 dependent furrow anti-correlates with the position of the spindle asters.
source: Whereas the position of the centralspindlin-dependent furrow correlates with the spindle midzone (Werner et al., 2007), the position of the NOP-1 dependent furrow anti-correlates with the position of the spindle asters (Hird and White, 1993; Dechant and Glotzer, 2003; Werner et al., 2007; Tse et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After fertilization, the sperm-derived centrosome serves as a symmetry-breaking cue that inhibits cortical contractility.
source: After fertilization, the sperm-derived centrosome serves as a symmetry-breaking cue that inhibits cortical contractility (Goldstein and Hird, 1996; Cowan and Hyman, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reduction in cortical contractility induces cortical flows that advect PAR proteins to the nascent anterior of the embryo.
source: This reduction in cortical contractility induces cortical flows that advect PAR proteins, such as PAR-3 and PAR-6, to the nascent anterior of the embryo (Munro et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Centrosomes locally concentrate Aurora A kinase (C.e. AIR-1), which is required for centrosome-directed displacement of the RhoGEF ECT-2 from the posterior cortex during polarization.
source: Centrosomes locally concentrate Aurora A kinase (C.e. AIR-1), which is required for centrosome-directed displacement of the RhoGEF ECT-2 from the posterior cortex during polarization (Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006; Zhao et al., 2019; Klinkert et al., 2019; Kapoor and Kotak, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ECT-2::mNG is well tolerated with >99% embryos hatching.
source: ECT-2::mNG is well tolerated (>99% embryos hatch).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study.

claim: During polarization, the cortical pool of ECT-2 increases and becomes progressively more asymmetric.
source: In the early zygote, the cortical pool of ECT-2 increases and it becomes progressively more asymmetric (Figure 1B i–iii).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The boundary length of the posterior domain where ECT-2 is displaced represents ~35% of the embryo at the time point of maximal ECT-2 asymmetry.
source: The size of the posterior domain where ECT-2 is displaced, that is, boundary length, represents ~35% of the embryo, measured at the time point of maximal ECT-2 asymmetry.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: ECT-2 accumulation on the anterior cortex is accompanied by an increase in cortical myosin accumulation.
source: ECT-2 accumulation on the anterior cortex is accompanied by an increase in cortical myosin accumulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), cortical contractility and pseudocleavage furrow formation, and transient elongation of the embryo (Figure 1B ii, v).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pseudocleavage furrow forms at the boundary between the myosin-enriched anterior and the myosin-depleted posterior of the embryo.
source: The pseudocleavage furrow forms at the boundary between the myosin-enriched anterior and the myosin-depleted posterior of the embryo; myosin does not solely accumulate at the furrow.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: During anaphase, ECT-2 again becomes preferentially displaced from the posterior ~35% of the embryo, becoming more asymmetric.
source: During anaphase, ECT-2 again becomes preferentially displaced from the posterior ~35% of the embryo, becoming more asymmetric (Figure 1C, 60 s, Figure 1D, i-iii).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: As furrow ingression begins, ECT-2 is not significantly enriched on the posterior cortex above its level in the cytoplasm.
source: As furrow ingression begins, ECT-2 is not significantly enriched on the posterior cortex above its level in the cytoplasm (Figure 1C 100 s).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A membrane probe, mCherry-PH, exhibits anterior enrichment, though to a lesser degree than ECT-2::mNG and its levels remain stable as anaphase progresses.
source: A membrane probe, mCherry-PH, which detects PIP2, also exhibits anterior enrichment, though to a lesser degree than ECT-2::mNG and its levels remain stable as anaphase progresses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Hirani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and a citation.

claim: Regional displacement of ECT-2 repeats in subsequent cell cycles.
source: Regional displacement of ECT-2 repeats in subsequent cell cycles; the cortical pool of ECT-2 decreases each cell cycle near spindle poles at anaphase and recovers in the subsequent cell cycles (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: As the spindle pole more closely approaches one region of the cortex, the ECT-2 on the cortex in that region is preferentially displaced following a short (~10 s) delay.
source: During spindle elongation, a correlation between spindle rocking and ECT-2 displacement is apparent: as the spindle pole more closely approaches one region of the cortex, the ECT-2 on the cortex in that region is preferentially displaced following a short (~10 s) delay (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Despite significant depletion of tubulin and near-complete depolymerization of microtubules, strong displacement of ECT-2 from a broad region of the posterior cortex is observed following mitotic exit.
source: Despite significant depletion of tubulin and near-complete depolymerization of microtubules (Figure 2B, insets), we observed strong displacement of ECT-2 from a broad region of the posterior cortex and the initiation of cortical contractility following mitotic exit (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ECT-2 becomes hyper-asymmetric in embryos depleted of tubulin and treated with nocodazole as compared to control embryos.
source: ECT-2 becomes hyper-asymmetric in these embryos as compared to control embryos and the depleted zone comprises a larger region of the embryo (Figure 2B), as is also observed in embryos with a diminished, posteriorly positioned spindle (see below).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ECT-2 asymmetry is reduced in embryos depleted of SPD-5 both during polarization and during cytokinesis.
source: ECT-2 asymmetry is reduced in these embryos both during polarization, as previously reported (Kapoor and Kotak, 2019), and during cytokinesis; in particular, significant ECT-2 remains on the posterior cortex (Figure 2C iii).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and a citation.

claim: Upon anaphase onset, embryos depleted of PAR-3 exhibit displacement of ECT-2 from both the anterior and posterior domains.
source: Upon anaphase onset, embryos depleted of PAR-3 exhibit displacement of ECT-2 from both the anterior and posterior domains (Figure 2D), indicating that both centrosomes are competent to inhibit ECT-2 accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both centrosomes are competent to inhibit ECT-2 accumulation.
source: Upon anaphase onset, embryos depleted of PAR-3 exhibit displacement of ECT-2 from both the anterior and posterior domains (Figure 2D), indicating that both centrosomes are competent to inhibit ECT-2 accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the PAR-3 depletion experiment.

claim: In Gα-depleted embryos, ECT-2 accumulation becomes nearly symmetric during anaphase rather than becoming more asymmetric as in the wild-type.
source: As a consequence, rather than ECT-2 accumulation becoming more asymmetric as anaphase progresses as in the wild-type, it becomes nearly symmetric.
evidence: This is an observation from the Gα depletion experiment.

claim: Displacement of ECT-2 from the cortex during cytokinesis is highly sensitive to centrosome-cortex separation.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that, during cytokinesis, displacement of ECT-2 from the cortex is highly sensitive to centrosome-cortex separation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments.

claim: In nop-1 mutant embryos, ECT-2:mNG accumulates asymmetrically, suggesting basal flow rates suffice.
source: In such embryos, ECT-2:mNG accumulates asymmetrically, suggesting basal flow rates suffice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In embryos with reduced myosin-dependent flows, ECT-2:mNG asymmetry is highly attenuated, though a local inhibitory effect on ECT-2:mNG accumulation in the immediate vicinity of the centrosome is detectable.
source: In embryos with reduced myosin-dependent flows, ECT-2:mNG asymmetry is highly attenuated, though a local inhibitory effect on ECT-2:mNG accumulation in the immediate vicinity of the centrosome is detectable; these results are consistent with an earlier report (Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006; Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and a citation.

claim: Cortical flows amplify the local, centrosome-induced reduction in cortical ECT-2 accumulation.
source: These results suggest that cortical flows amplify the local, centrosome-induced reduction in cortical ECT-2 accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the myosin depletion experiments.

claim: ECT-2 displacement and asymmetric accumulation was not abolished by reduction of NOP-1 and CYK-4 functions during cytokinesis.
source: ECT-2 displacement and asymmetric accumulation was not abolished by these perturbations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Basal levels of RHO-1 activation suffice to promote displacement of ECT-2 from the posterior cortex during anaphase.
source: Thus, basal levels of RHO-1 activation suffice to promote displacement of ECT-2 from the posterior cortex during anaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NOP-1 and CYK-4 depletion experiments.

claim: In zyg-9(b244ts) embryos, during anaphase, ECT-2 becomes hyper-asymmetric with a stronger reduction in the posterior cortical pool of ECT-2, an increase in the anterior cortical pool, and an expansion of the posterior domain depleted of ECT-2.
source: Under these conditions, during anaphase, ECT-2 becomes hyper-asymmetric with a stronger reduction in the posterior cortical pool of ECT-2, an increase in the anterior cortical pool, and an expansion of the posterior domain depleted of ECT-2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cortical flows contribute to ECT-2 asymmetry.
source: We conclude that cortical flows contribute to ECT-2 asymmetry.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments.

claim: Asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation is not abrogated by depletion of the heavy chain of cytoplasmic dynein, DHC-1.
source: However, asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation is not abrogated by depletion the heavy chain of cytoplasmic dynein, DHC-1.
evidence: This is an observation from the DHC-1 depletion experiment.

claim: DHC-1 depletion causes enhanced ECT-2 asymmetry, presumably due to the close association of the centrosomes with the posterior cortex.
source: To the contrary, DHC-1 depletion, which would be predicted to compromise dynein-mediated stripping of cortical myosin, causes enhanced ECT-2 asymmetry, akin to the situation in embryos in which microtubule assembly is strongly suppressed, presumably due to the close association of the centrosomes with the posterior cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increases or decreases in cortical flows enhance or attenuate the extent of ECT-2 asymmetry, respectively.
source: Thus, not only are cortical flows required for asymmetric ECT-2, increases or decreases in cortical flows enhance or attenuate the extent of ECT-2 asymmetry, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments.

claim: Following bleaching, ECT-2:mNG rapidly recovers with a t1/2 of ~3 s.
source: Following bleaching, ECT-2:mNG rapidly recovers with a t1/2 of ~3 s; with no obvious difference detected between polarization and cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a measurement from FRAP experiments.

claim: ECT-2 asymmetry is likely to reflect the dynamic association of ECT-2 with more stably associated cortical component(s) that undergo cortical flow.
source: We conclude that ECT-2 asymmetry is likely to reflect the dynamic association of ECT-2 with more stably associated cortical component(s) that undergo cortical flow (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In ZYG-9-deficient embryos, only ~50% of ECT-2 on the posterior furrow recovers in FRAP experiments, whereas the anterior furrow more fully recovers.
source: FRAP analysis of the posterior and anterior furrows indicates that in both cases the mobile fraction of ECT-2 recovers quickly, but only ~50% of ECT-2 on the posterior furrow recovers, whereas the anterior furrow more fully recovers (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Depletion of AIR-1 by RNAi reduces, but does not abolish, ECT-2 asymmetry during cytokinesis.
source: As a consequence, depletion of AIR-1 by RNAi reduces, but does not abolish, ECT-2 asymmetry during cytokinesis (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The residual asymmetry in ECT-2 accumulation in AIR-1-depleted embryos is further reduced by co-depletion of PAR-2.
source: The residual asymmetry in ECT-2 accumulation in AIR-1-depleted embryos is further reduced by co-depletion of PAR-2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In embryos deficient in both ZYG-9 and AIR-1, the spindle does not induce the pronounced ECT-2 asymmetry observed in the presence of AIR-1.
source: Although the spindle assembles close to the posterior pole, it does not induce the pronounced ECT-2 asymmetry observed in the presence of AIR-1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: AIR-1 promotes displacement of ECT-2 from the cortex during anaphase.
source: We conclude that AIR-1 promotes displacement of ECT-2 from the cortex during anaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments.

claim: Treatment of embryos with MLN8237 at metaphase resulted in a rapid enhancement in cortical ECT-2 accumulation during cytokinesis.
source: Treatment of embryos with MLN8237 at metaphase resulted in a rapid enhancement in cortical ECT-2 accumulation during cytokinesis, indicating that AIR-1 functions during anaphase to promote ECT-2 displacement from the cortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: AIR-1 functions during anaphase to promote ECT-2 displacement from the cortex.
source: Treatment of embryos with MLN8237 at metaphase resulted in a rapid enhancement in cortical ECT-2 accumulation during cytokinesis, indicating that AIR-1 functions during anaphase to promote ECT-2 displacement from the cortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MLN8237 inhibitor experiment.

claim: Overall cortical ECT-2 accumulation is enhanced by TPXL-1 depletion, though the degree of ECT-2 asymmetry is unaffected.
source: Overall cortical ECT-2 accumulation is enhanced by TPXL-1 depletion, though the degree of ECT-2 asymmetry is unaffected (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Robust depletion of ECT-2 at the posterior pole is observed in zyg-9(b244) embryos depleted of TPXL-1, but not AIR-1.
source: Under these conditions, we observed robust depletion of ECT-2 at the posterior pole in zyg-9(b244) embryos depleted of TPXL-1, but not AIR-1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: While AIR-1 is a major regulator of the asymmetric accumulation of ECT-2, the TPXL-1/AIR-1 complex does not play a central role in this process.
source: We conclude that while AIR-1 is a major regulator of the asymmetric accumulation of ECT-2, the TPXL-1/AIR-1 complex does not play a central role in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TPXL-1 depletion experiments.

claim: SAPS-1 depletion results in an overall reduction in cortical ECT-2.
source: As expected for a negative regulator of AIR-1, SAPS-1 depletion results in an overall reduction in cortical ECT-2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The cortical pool of ECT-2 remains somewhat asymmetric in SAPS-1-depleted embryos.
source: Nevertheless, the cortical pool of ECT-2 remains somewhat asymmetric in SAPS-1-depleted embryos.
evidence: This is an observation from the SAPS-1 depletion experiment.

claim: AIR-1 activity inhibits cortical association of ECT-2.
source: These results indicate that AIR-1 activity inhibits cortical association of ECT-2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SAPS-1 depletion experiments.

claim: A C-terminal fragment of ECT-2 that extends from the N-terminus of the DH domain to the C-terminus exhibits cortical accumulation.
source: As previously shown, a C-terminal fragment of ECT-2 that extends from the N-terminus of the DH domain to the C-terminus exhibits cortical accumulation (Chan and Nance, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cortical accumulation of ECT-2 is independent of the majority of the DH domain, but required both the PH domain and a portion of the region C-terminal to the PH domain.
source: Further deletion analysis indicates that cortical accumulation is independent of the majority of the DH domain, but required both the PH domain and a portion of the region C-terminal to the PH domain, but not its entirety (ECT-2C) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The accumulation pattern of ECT-2C is similar to that of endogenous ECT-2 during both polarization and cytokinesis.
source: The accumulation pattern of ECT-2C is similar to that of endogenous ECT-2 during both polarization and cytokinesis (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: AIR-1 depletion resulted in a reduction in the degree of asymmetric accumulation of ECT-2C.
source: AIR-1 depletion resulted in a reduction in the degree of its asymmetric accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C-terminal fragment of ECT-2 is sufficient to respond to the inhibitory signal from the centrosomes.
source: These data indicate that this C-terminal fragment of ECT-2 is sufficient to respond to the inhibitory signal from the centrosomes, and that the N-terminal regulatory domain and the DH domain of ECT-2 are dispensable for asymmetric ECT-2, and its recruitment by centralspindlin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ECT-2C experiments.

claim: The N-terminal regulatory domain and the DH domain of ECT-2 are dispensable for asymmetric ECT-2 and its recruitment by centralspindlin.
source: These data indicate that this C-terminal fragment of ECT-2 is sufficient to respond to the inhibitory signal from the centrosomes, and that the N-terminal regulatory domain and the DH domain of ECT-2 are dispensable for asymmetric ECT-2, and its recruitment by centralspindlin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ECT-2C experiments.

claim: Both ECT-2C variants with alanine substitutions at putative AIR-1 sites exhibited increased cortical accumulation as compared to ECT-2C.
source: As compared to ECT-2C, both variants with alanine substitutions exhibited increased cortical accumulation (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: ECT-2C variants with alanine substitutions accumulated in an asymmetric manner.
source: Nevertheless, these variants accumulated in an asymmetric manner.
evidence: This is an observation from the ECT-2C mutant experiments.

claim: In the absence of myosin-dependent flows, the degree of GFP:ECT-2C asymmetry is dramatically attenuated.
source: In the absence of myosin-dependent flows, the degree of GFP:ECT-2C asymmetry is dramatically attenuated (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In 7/9 embryos depleted of myosin, a local inhibitory effect in the immediate vicinity of the centrosome is detectable for GFP:ECT-2C.
source: In 7/9 embryos, however, a local inhibitory effect in the immediate vicinity of the centrosome is detectable.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the myosin depletion experiment.

claim: Under myosin depletion conditions, only 1/10 ECT-2C_3A embryos exhibit significant displacement near the centrosome.
source: In contrast, under these conditions, only 1/10 ECT-2C_3A embryos exhibit significant displacement near the centrosome.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the myosin depletion experiment.

claim: Centrosome-associated AIR-1 locally inhibits cortical ECT-2 accumulation.
source: These results suggest that centrosome-associated AIR-1 locally inhibits cortical ECT-2 accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ECT-2C mutant and myosin depletion experiments.

claim: Upon anaphase onset, GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 induces displacement of GFP:ECT-2C.
source: Upon anaphase onset, GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 induces displacement of GFP:ECT-2C (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: GFP:ECT-2C_3A is refractory to GBP::mCherry::AIR-1-induced displacement.
source: Importantly, GFP:ECT-2C_3A is refractory to GBP::mCherry::AIR-1-induced displacement (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: AIR-1 directly modulates ECT-2 localization by phosphorylation of residues within a loop in the PH domain.
source: These results support the hypothesis that AIR-1 directly modulates ECT-2 localization by phosphorylation of residues within a loop in the PH domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 experiments.

claim: Embryos deficient in centralspindlin subunits form ingressing, NOP-1-dependent furrows during cytokinesis which fail to form upon depletion of SAPS-1/PPH-6.
source: For example, embryos deficient in centralspindlin subunits form ingressing, NOP-1-dependent furrows during cytokinesis which fail to form upon depletion of SAPS-1/PPH-6, a complex that negatively regulates AIR-1 (Afshar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Depletion of AIR-1 results in ectopic furrows during pseudocleavage and cytokinesis.
source: Conversely, depletion of AIR-1 results in ectopic furrows during pseudocleavage (Kapoor and Kotak, 2019) and cytokinesis (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NOP-1 is required for ectopic furrows in AIR-1-depleted embryos.
source: NOP-1, the upstream-most factor in the centralspindlin-independent pathway (Tse et al., 2012), is required for these ectopic furrows (Kapoor and Kotak, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Embryos triply deficient in AIR-1, CYK-4, and NOP-1 fail to furrow during anaphase.
source: To that end, we depleted both AIR-1 and CYK-4 in nop-1(it142) embryos. These triply deficient embryos fail to furrow during anaphase (100%, n=8).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study.

claim: While 100% of embryos deficient in NOP-1 furrow to completion, ~30% embryos deficient in both AIR-1 and NOP-1 ingress with markedly slower kinetics and some fail to complete ingression.
source: While 100% of embryos deficient in NOP-1 furrow to completion, ~30% embryos deficient in both AIR-1 and NOP-1 ingress with markedly slower kinetics and some fail to complete ingression (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: While AIR-1 primarily impacts NOP-1-directed furrowing, it also affects centralspindlin-directed furrowing.
source: These results suggest that while AIR-1 primarily impacts NOP-1-directed furrowing, it also affects centralspindlin-directed furrowing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AIR-1 and NOP-1 depletion experiments.

claim: Cortical accumulation of ECT-2T634E is reduced and less asymmetric.
source: This strain could be readily maintained as a homozygote (>98% hatch rate), indicating that this allele retains significant function, although cortical accumulation of ECT-2T634E is reduced and less asymmetric.
evidence: This is an observation from the ECT-2T634E mutant.

claim: Reduction of ECT-2:mNG levels to ~20% of wild-type results in cytokinesis failure in only ~11% of embryos.
source: Reduction of ECT-2:mNG levels to ~20% of wild-type results in cytokinesis failure in only ~11% of embryos.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the partial ECT-2 depletion experiment.

claim: In the wild-type, ECT-2 accumulates to levels in excess of that required for completion of cytokinesis.
source: Thus, in the wild-type, ECT-2 accumulates to levels in excess of that required for completion of cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the partial ECT-2 depletion experiment.

claim: A similar reduction of ECT-2T634E:mNG results in cytokinesis failure in ~50% of embryos.
source: In contrast, a similar reduction of ECT-2T634E:mNG results in cytokinesis failure in ~50% of embryos, suggesting that phosphorylation of ECT-2 on T634 attenuates ECT-2 function.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the partial ECT-2T634E depletion experiment.

claim: Phosphorylation of ECT-2 on T634 attenuates ECT-2 function.
source: In contrast, a similar reduction of ECT-2T634E:mNG results in cytokinesis failure in ~50% of embryos, suggesting that phosphorylation of ECT-2 on T634 attenuates ECT-2 function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the partial ECT-2T634E depletion experiment.

claim: ECT-2T634E:mNG slows the rate of furrow ingression as compared to wild-type, but furrow initiation is not delayed.
source: Importantly, whereas ECT-2T634E:mNG slows the rate of furrow ingression as compared to wild-type, furrow initiation is not delayed.
evidence: This is an observation from the ECT-2T634E mutant.

claim: Partial depletion of ECT-2 does not affect the rate of furrow ingression, but it delays furrow initiation.
source: In contrast, partial depletion of ECT-2 does not affect the rate of furrow ingression, but it delays furrow initiation.
evidence: This is an observation from the partial ECT-2 depletion experiment.

claim: The defects resulting from the T634E substitution are distinct from those resulting from an overall reduction in ECT-2 function.
source: These results suggest that the defects resulting from the T634E substitution are distinct from those resulting from an overall reduction in ECT-2 function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing ECT-2T634E and partial ECT-2 depletion.

claim: ECT-2:mNG embryos depleted of NOP-1 complete cytokinesis with only a slight delay.
source: Whereas ECT-2:mNG embryos depleted of NOP-1 complete cytokinesis with only a slight delay, embryos expressing ECT-2T634E and depleted of NOP-1 exhibit highly variable furrowing behavior.
evidence: This is an observation from the NOP-1 depletion experiment.

claim: Embryos expressing ECT-2T634E and depleted of NOP-1 exhibit highly variable furrowing behavior.
source: Whereas ECT-2:mNG embryos depleted of NOP-1 complete cytokinesis with only a slight delay, embryos expressing ECT-2T634E and depleted of NOP-1 exhibit highly variable furrowing behavior.
evidence: This is an observation from the NOP-1 depletion experiment in ECT-2T634E embryos.

claim: The introduction of a single phosphomimetic residue at a putative AIR-1 site in a flexible loop in the PH domain of ECT-2 impairs centralspindlin-dependent furrowing.
source: We conclude that the introduction of a single phosphomimetic residue at a putative AIR-1 site in a flexible loop in the PH domain of ECT-2 impairs centralspindlin-dependent furrowing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ECT-2T634E experiments.

claim: An inhibitory cue associated with centrosomes triggers a local, Aurora A kinase-dependent inhibition of cortical ECT-2 recruitment.
source: Here, we show that an inhibitory cue associated with centrosomes triggers a local, Aurora A kinase-dependent inhibition of cortical ECT-2 recruitment (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by Figure 7A.

claim: The posteriorly shifted spindle triggers preferential displacement of ECT-2 from the posterior cortex by Aurora A-dependent phosphorylation of the ECT-2 PH domain.
source: Our studies suggest that the posteriorly shifted spindle triggers preferential displacement of ECT-2 from the posterior cortex by Aurora A-dependent phosphorylation of the ECT-2 PH domain, though the evidence for this phosphorylation event is indirect.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study with acknowledgment that evidence is indirect.

claim: Local inhibition of cortical ECT-2 recruitment triggers anterior-directed, myosin-dependent cortical flows that amplify ECT-2 asymmetric accumulation.
source: This local inhibition of cortical ECT-2 recruitment triggers anterior-directed, myosin-dependent cortical flows that amplify ECT-2 asymmetric accumulation, likely generating positive feedback (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study, supported by Figure 7B.

claim: Inhibition of cortical accumulation of ECT-2 by Aurora A influences both centralspindlin-independent and -dependent furrowing.
source: Inhibition of cortical accumulation of ECT-2 by Aurora A influences both centralspindlin-independent and -dependent furrowing.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study.

claim: During cytokinesis, ECT-2 accumulation and centrosome proximity inversely correlate over a range of distances up to ~20 µm (40% of embryo length).
source: These data demonstrate that, during cytokinesis, ECT-2 accumulation and centrosome proximity inversely correlate over a range of distances up to ~20 µm (40% of embryo length).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The inhibitory effect of centrosomes on ECT-2 accumulation decays rapidly in the range of 10–18 µm from the cortex.
source: The inhibitory effect of centrosomes on ECT-2 accumulation decays rapidly in the range of 10–18 µm from the cortex, which correspond to the positions of the posterior and anterior centrosomes in wild-type embryos (Kemphues et al., 1988), respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis shown in Figure 7A and a citation.

claim: In wild-type embryos, Aurora A-dependent symmetry breaking is amplified by anterior-directed cortical flows that enhance ECT-2 asymmetry.
source: These results suggest that in wild-type embryos, Aurora A-dependent symmetry breaking is amplified by anterior-directed cortical flows that enhance ECT-2 asymmetry.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study.

claim: Centrosomal AIR-1 not only breaks symmetry, but this regulation of ECT-2 by centrosomal AIR-1 continues throughout anaphase.
source: Further, we speculate that centrosomal AIR-1 not only breaks symmetry, but that this regulation of ECT-2 by centrosomal AIR-1 continues throughout anaphase.
evidence: This is stated as speculation.

claim: Asymmetric ECT-2 is predicted to enhance asymmetric assembly of cortical myosin, which is predicted to accentuate cortical flows, further amplifying ECT-2 asymmetry.
source: Furthermore, asymmetric ECT-2 is predicted to enhance asymmetric assembly of cortical myosin, which is predicted to accentuate cortical flows, further amplifying ECT-2 asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction/speculation.

claim: The association of ECT-2 with the cortex involves interactions with cortical component(s) that are concentrated by cortical flows.
source: Rather, we favor a model in which the association of ECT-2 with the cortex involves interactions with cortical component(s) that are concentrated by cortical flows (Mayer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a proposed model with a citation.

claim: The PH domain of ECT-2 has been shown to bind the actomyosin-binding protein anillin.
source: The PH domain of ECT-2 has been shown to bind the actomyosin-binding protein anillin (Frenette et al., 2012), making it a candidate contributor to ECT-2 cortical anchoring.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Basal levels of myosin appear sufficient to drive the cortical flows that polarize ECT-2.
source: Although RhoGEF activators accelerate cortical flows, basal levels of myosin appear sufficient to drive the cortical flows that polarize ECT-2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NOP-1 experiments.

claim: Cortical flow-mediated concentration of ECT-2 may be central to polarization of the embryo.
source: Cortical flow-mediated concentration of ECT-2 may be central to polarization of the embryo, analogous to flow-induced re-orientation of PAR protein polarity (Mittasch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility with a citation.

claim: During anaphase, asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation is myosin-dependent, presumably due to its role in generating cortical flows.
source: During anaphase, asymmetric ECT-2 accumulation is also myosin-dependent, presumably due to its role in generating cortical flows.
evidence: This is a conclusion with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Bulk, cortical ECT-2 has a low level of RhoGEF activity.
source: We infer that bulk, cortical ECT-2 has a low level of RhoGEF activity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference.

claim: The temporal pattern of ECT-2 cortical accumulation is dynamic.
source: The temporal pattern of ECT-2 cortical accumulation is dynamic.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Cell cycle regulated, global changes in ECT-2 accumulation are apparent in AIR-1-depleted embryos.
source: For example, cell cycle regulated, global changes in ECT-2 accumulation are apparent in AIR-1-depleted embryos.
evidence: This is an observation from AIR-1-depleted embryos.

claim: The ability of GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 to induce GFP-ECT-2C displacement fluctuates with the cell cycle.
source: Furthermore, the ability of GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 to induce GFP-ECT-2C displacement fluctuates with the cell cycle, suggesting the susceptibility of ECT-2 to AIR-1 may be cell cycle regulated.
evidence: This is an observation with an inference.

claim: The susceptibility of ECT-2 to AIR-1 may be cell cycle regulated.
source: Furthermore, the ability of GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 to induce GFP-ECT-2C displacement fluctuates with the cell cycle, suggesting the susceptibility of ECT-2 to AIR-1 may be cell cycle regulated.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion/speculation.

claim: TPXL-1 makes a more modest contribution to ECT-2 asymmetry than does AIR-1.
source: However, TPXL-1 makes a more modest contribution to ECT-2 asymmetry than does AIR-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing AIR-1 and TPXL-1 depletion experiments.

claim: TPXL-1 is dispensable for ECT-2 asymmetry when spindle poles are close to the cortex.
source: Indeed, TPXL-1 is dispensable for ECT-2 asymmetry when spindle poles are close to the cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TPXL-1 depletion experiments in zyg-9 mutants.

claim: Several AIR-1 functions, particularly those at the centrosome, are TPXL-1 independent.
source: This finding is consistent with earlier work that revealed that several AIR-1 functions, particularly those at the centrosome, are TPXL-1 independent (Ozlü et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AIR-1 appears to regulate Rho-mediated contractility at multiple steps, which are differentially dependent on both TPXL-1 and NMY-2.
source: Thus, AIR-1 appears to regulate Rho-mediated contractility at multiple steps, which are differentially dependent on both TPXL-1 and NMY-2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different experiments.

claim: Cortical recruitment of ECT-2 can occur by two distinct modes: one independent of centralspindlin and inhibited by AIR-1, and another dependent on centralspindlin and less sensitive to AIR-1 activity.
source: These results indicate that cortical recruitment of ECT-2 can occur by two distinct modes. One mode is independent of centralspindlin, and is inhibited by AIR-1. The other mode is dependent on centralspindlin and is less sensitive to AIR-1 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments.

claim: Centralspindlin-dependent accumulation of cortical ECT-2 correlates with a reduced mobile fraction of ECT-2 as compared to the ECT-2 that accumulates on the cortex more broadly.
source: The centralspindlin-dependent mode of ECT-2 accumulation correlates with a reduced mobile fraction of ECT-2 as compared to the ECT-2 that accumulates on the cortex more broadly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FRAP experiments.

claim: In both C. elegans and human cells, phosphorylation of the C-terminus of ECT-2 attenuates its cortical association.
source: Thus, in both systems, phosphorylation of the C-terminus of ECT-2 attenuates its cortical association.
evidence: This is a comparison between C. elegans and human cells.

claim: The kinases that phosphorylate ECT-2 are distinct (Cdk1 in human cells vs. AIR-1 in C. elegans).
source: However, the kinases are distinct (Cdk1 in human cells vs. AIR-1 in C. elegans) whereas the phosphoregulation appears global in human cells and spatially regulated in C. elegans blastomeres.
evidence: This is a comparison between C. elegans and human cells.

claim: Phosphoregulation of ECT-2 appears global in human cells and spatially regulated in C. elegans blastomeres.
source: However, the kinases are distinct (Cdk1 in human cells vs. AIR-1 in C. elegans) whereas the phosphoregulation appears global in human cells and spatially regulated in C. elegans blastomeres.
evidence: This is a comparison between C. elegans and human cells.

claim: Inhibition of ECT-2 accumulation by centrosomal Aurora A at spindle poles can induce furrow formation.
source: The results shown here indicate that inhibition of ECT-2 accumulation by centrosomal Aurora A at spindle poles can induce furrow formation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Aurora A and Aurora B regulate cytokinesis in quite different manners.
source: Remarkably, the highly similar kinases, Aurora A and Aurora B, regulate cytokinesis in quite different manners.
evidence: This is a general statement based on the study and prior knowledge.

claim: Aurora A primarily acts to inhibit contractility at cell poles through ECT-2.
source: Aurora A primarily acts to inhibit contractility at cell poles through ECT-2, while Aurora B primarily promotes contractility at the equator through centralspindlin (Basant et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study with a citation.

claim: Aurora B primarily promotes contractility at the equator through centralspindlin.
source: Aurora A primarily acts to inhibit contractility at cell poles through ECT-2, while Aurora B primarily promotes contractility at the equator through centralspindlin (Basant et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.
